stem: What is the primary purpose of an Application Load Balancer (ALB) in AWS?
options: To distribute TCP traffic across multiple targets
To perform health checks on target instances
To route HTTP/HTTPS traffic based on rules
To provide static IP addresses for services
explanation: An Application Load Balancer (ALB) primarily routes HTTP/HTTPS traffic based on rules, such as path-based or host-based routing.

stem: What is the primary function of Amazon Route 53?
options: To provide a firewall for AWS resources
To manage virtual private networks
To offer DNS services and routing policies
To create and manage load balancers
explanation: Amazon Route 53 is primarily a DNS service that offers various routing policies for domain name resolution and traffic management.

stem: Which of the following routing policies is NOT supported by AWS Route 53?
options: Weighted routing
Geolocation routing
Failover routing
Round robin routing
explanation: Round robin routing is not explicitly listed as a routing policy in AWS Route 53; it uses weighted, geolocation, and failover routing instead.

stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of cross-zone load balancing in AWS?
options: It is enabled by default for Application Load Balancers
It distributes traffic evenly across all registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones
It can only be used with Network Load Balancers
It requires manual configuration for each target group
explanation: Cross-zone load balancing distributes traffic evenly across all registered targets in all enabled Availability Zones, ensuring better resource utilization.

stem: What is the purpose of health checks in AWS load balancers?
options: To ensure that all instances are always online
To determine the health of targets before routing traffic
To monitor network latency
To configure security group rules
explanation: Health checks in AWS load balancers are used to determine the health of targets before routing traffic to them, ensuring that only healthy instances receive traffic.

stem: What is the difference between a CNAME record and an ALIAS record in Route 53?
options: CNAME can point to an A record; ALIAS cannot
ALIAS can point to AWS resources, while CNAME cannot
CNAME is used for root domains; ALIAS is for subdomains
ALIAS records do not support DNS failover
explanation: ALIAS records can point to AWS resources like CloudFront distributions or S3 buckets, while CNAME records cannot be used at the root domain level.

stem: Which of the following best describes a Network Load Balancer (NLB) in AWS?
options: Operates at Layer 7 and routes based on HTTP headers
Provides ultra-low latency and operates at Layer 4
Can only distribute traffic to EC2 instances
Requires SSL termination for secure traffic
explanation: A Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at Layer 4 and provides ultra-low latency for TCP/UDP traffic.

stem: At which OSI layer does an Application Load Balancer make routing decisions such as forwarding requests by URL path?
options: Layer 3
Layer 7
Layer 4 only
Layer 2
explanation: As the lesson 'Classic and Application Load Balancers' explains (chapter 'Application Load Balancer: Target Groups and Setup', 62:37), the ALB works at the application layer and can route by content, path or host. Path-based routing needs the HTTP request, which a Layer 4 device does not inspect.

stem: An application must send example.com/images to one group of servers and example.com/videos to another. Which design meets this?
options: A Classic Load Balancer with two HTTP listeners on port 80
A Network Load Balancer with path-based listener rules
An Application Load Balancer with listener rules that forward each path to its own target group
An Application Load Balancer with one target group whose health check path is /images
explanation: As the lesson 'Classic and Application Load Balancers' explains (chapter 'Application Load Balancer: Target Groups and Setup', 62:37), an ALB routes by path to different target groups, which suits microservices such as /images and /videos. A Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4 and cannot read paths, and a health check path does not route traffic.

stem: Which records does Route 53 create automatically when a new public hosted zone is created? (Choose two)
options: NS record
A record for the zone apex
MX record
SOA record
CNAME record for www
explanation: As the lesson 'Amazon Route 53 and CloudWatch Overview' explains (chapter 'Hosted Zones', 32:03), a new hosted zone starts with two records: NS, listing the name servers, and SOA, holding zone administration information. A, MX and CNAME records must be created by the administrator.

stem: A private hosted zone corp.internal resolves from instances in VPC-A but not from instances in VPC-B, which is in the same account and region. Which are likely causes? (Choose two)
options: The private hosted zone is not associated with VPC-B
The zone has no NS delegation at a public domain registrar
DNS resolution (enableDnsSupport) is disabled on VPC-B
The records use simple routing instead of weighted routing
A private hosted zone can be associated with only one VPC
explanation: As the lesson 'Amazon Route 53 and CloudWatch Overview' explains (chapter 'Hosted Zones', 32:03), a private hosted zone resolves only inside the VPCs it is associated with, and a VPC needs DNS resolution enabled to use it. A private zone can be associated with many VPCs and never needs public delegation, and the routing policy does not limit which VPCs can resolve it.

stem: How does Azure Traffic Manager direct users to an endpoint?
options: It proxies every HTTP request through its own servers
It answers DNS queries with the chosen endpoint, and the client then connects directly to that endpoint
It distributes TCP flows at Layer 4 inside a single region
It caches static files at edge locations near users
explanation: As the lesson 'Azure Traffic Manager and Storage Accounts' explains (chapter 'Introduction to Traffic Manager and Load Balancer Comparison', 00:44), Traffic Manager is a DNS-based global load balancer that uses DNS resolution to send users to an endpoint. It never sits in the data path; Layer 4 flow distribution in one region is what Azure Load Balancer does.

stem: A Traffic Manager profile uses Priority routing: the East US web app has priority 1 and the Japan East web app has priority 2. Endpoint monitoring marks East US as degraded. What do new DNS queries receive?
options: No answer until an administrator changes the priorities
Both endpoints, alternating in round-robin
The Japan East endpoint, until East US is healthy again
The East US endpoint, because priority 1 is always returned
explanation: As the lesson 'Azure Traffic Manager and Storage Accounts' explains (chapter 'Traffic Manager Concepts and Routing Methods', 13:35), Priority routing sends traffic to the primary endpoint and falls back to the secondary when the primary is down. Traffic Manager skips unhealthy endpoints automatically, so priority 1 is not returned while it is degraded.

stem: Users worldwide should be sent to the endpoint that gives them the lowest network latency. Which Traffic Manager routing method fits?
options: Performance
Geographic
Weighted
Priority
explanation: As the lesson 'Azure Traffic Manager and Storage Accounts' explains (chapter 'Traffic Manager Concepts and Routing Methods', 13:35), Performance routing sends users to the endpoint with the best observed response time. Geographic routing maps users to endpoints by where their DNS query comes from (for example for data residency), which is not the same as lowest latency.

stem: Which two statements correctly compare Azure Load Balancer and Azure Traffic Manager? (Choose two)
options: Traffic Manager terminates TLS and inspects HTTP headers before forwarding requests
A regional Azure Load Balancer distributes TCP and UDP flows at Layer 4 within one region
Traffic Manager works at the DNS level and can send users to endpoints in different regions
Azure Load Balancer returns DNS answers to send users to other continents
Traffic Manager requires all endpoints to be in the same virtual network
explanation: As the lesson 'Azure Traffic Manager and Storage Accounts' explains (chapter 'Introduction to Traffic Manager and Load Balancer Comparison', 00:44), Load Balancer works at Layer 4 within a region while Traffic Manager works at DNS level across regions. Traffic Manager never terminates TLS, and its endpoints are deliberately spread over different regions rather than one VNet.

stem: An NGINX upstream block lists two servers with no load-balancing method and no weights. How does open-source NGINX distribute requests?
options: Round-robin, alternating between the two servers
By a hash of the client's source IP address
To the server with the fewest active connections
All to the first server, using the second only when the first fails
explanation: As the lesson 'NGINX Reverse Proxy, Load Balancing and Caching' demonstrates (chapter 'Nginx Load Balancing Configuration', 50:02), the default method is round-robin, which split requests evenly between server 1 and server 2. ip_hash and least_conn must be configured explicitly, and a standby server needs the backup parameter.

stem: In a two-server NGINX upstream with default settings, NGINX is stopped on server 2, and repeated curl requests to the load balancer now return only server 1's page. What explains this?
options: Open-source NGINX actively probes every upstream server every 5 seconds
The upstream switched to ip_hash automatically after the failure
Passive health checking marks server 2 unavailable after failed attempts (max_fails, default 1, within fail_timeout, default 10 seconds) and sends traffic to the healthy server
The client's DNS cache still resolves the load balancer to server 1
explanation: As the lesson 'NGINX Reverse Proxy, Load Balancing and Caching' explains (chapter 'Health Checks in Load Balancing', 81:26), open-source NGINX has built-in passive health checks that stop sending traffic to an unresponsive server. Active health checks require NGINX Plus, and NGINX never changes the balancing method on its own.

stem: What does a load balancer present to clients when it virtualizes a service hosted on several backend servers?
options: A separate public IP address for each backend server, returned in rotation by DNS
A single IP address and port that represents the whole group of servers
The MAC address of the least busy server, learned through ARP
A 3xx redirect to the backend server that should handle the request
explanation: As the lesson 'Load Balancing and ADC Fundamentals' explains (chapter 'Understanding Load Balancing: Definition and Purpose', 02:56), load balancing presents one IP address and port to the outside world so that many physical servers appear as one large server. Returning a different address per server in rotation is DNS round robin, not a virtualized service.

stem: A company publishes www.example.com with three A records and relies on DNS round robin. One web server hangs: it still answers ping but no longer serves HTTP. What happens to clients?
options: The DNS server detects the hung service and stops returning that server's address
The remaining servers automatically redirect affected clients with a 3xx response
The client resolver removes the address from its cache after the first failed TCP connection
Some clients still receive the hung server's address and their requests fail, because DNS does not check server or service health
explanation: As the lesson 'Load Balancing and ADC Fundamentals' explains (chapter 'Understanding Load Balancing: Definition and Purpose', 02:56), DNS round robin only rotates the addresses it returns and cannot detect a failed server or a hung service, so traffic keeps going to the unresponsive server. A load balancer or ADC fixes this with health checks.

stem: A banking portal runs on four servers behind an ADC. One server's operating system crashes during business hours. Which ADC behaviour keeps the portal available?
options: Periodic health checks mark the failed server down, and new requests are sent only to the healthy servers
The ADC restarts the crashed server's operating system through its management port
The ADC lowers the DNS TTL so that clients re-resolve to a different server
The ADC queues requests for the failed server until it comes back online
explanation: As the lesson 'Load Balancing and ADC Fundamentals' explains (chapter 'High Availability and Predictability in Load Balancing', 11:32), load balancers provide high availability by health-checking backend servers and redirecting traffic away from failed ones. Queuing requests for a dead server would cause exactly the outage high availability is meant to prevent.

stem: Which three capabilities of an Application Delivery Controller go beyond what DNS round-robin load balancing can provide? (Choose three)
options: Returning several A records for one name in a rotating order
Verifying backend server health so that traffic is sent only to healthy servers
Directing a request to a server optimised for the client's device type
Relying on client resolver caches to spread users across servers
Modifying a request before it reaches the backend server
explanation: As the lesson 'Load Balancing and ADC Fundamentals' explains (chapter 'Application Delivery Controllers (ADCs) and Their Capabilities', 13:38), an ADC directs or redirects requests by criteria such as device type, can modify requests in transit, and verifies server health. Rotating A records and depending on resolver caches are how DNS round robin works, without any of those controls.

stem: Which two statements correctly describe BIG-IP monitor check types? (Choose two)
options: An address check sends ICMP echo requests to the node's IP address
A service check verifies that the HTTP response body contains an expected receive string
A service check opens a TCP connection to the IP address and port and expects a SYN-ACK
An in-band monitor sends a synthetic HTTP request to every pool member at each interval
A content check only confirms that the node answers ICMP
explanation: As the lesson 'Traffic Management Shell (TMSH) and Health Monitors' explains (chapter 'Types of Monitors and Configuration Settings', 44:12), an address check uses ICMP to test node reachability, a service check opens a TCP connection to the IP and port expecting a SYN-ACK, and a content check sends commands such as an HTTP request and examines the response. An in-band monitor is passive: it judges health from real client connections rather than sending its own probes.

stem: A pool member uses an HTTP monitor with an interval of 5 seconds and a timeout of 16 seconds. At 10:00:00 the application stops responding; the last successful check arrived just before that. When does the BIG-IP mark the member down?
options: At about 10:00:05, after the first missed check
At about 10:00:16, when no successful response has arrived within the 16-second timeout, after several missed checks
At about 10:00:25, after five consecutive missed checks
Never, because a timeout larger than the interval prevents the monitor from failing
explanation: As the lesson 'Traffic Management Shell (TMSH) and Health Monitors' explains (chapter 'Monitor Interval, Timeout, and Best Practices', 49:18), with a 5-second interval and 16-second timeout the BIG-IP probes every 5 seconds and marks the resource down only when no successful response arrives within 16 seconds, which allows roughly three missed probes. F5 recommends a timeout of three times the interval plus one second (the 5 and 16 of the default HTTP monitor), so one missed probe does not take the member down.

stem: Pool web_pool, used by virtual server vs_web, has members 10.1.1.10:80 and 10.1.1.11:80. A node-level ICMP monitor on node 10.1.1.10 fails, while 10.1.1.11 passes all its monitors. Which two results follow? (Choose two)
options: Virtual server vs_web is marked down because one member is down
Member 10.1.1.10:80 is marked down because its node is down
Member 10.1.1.11:80 is also marked down, because members inherit status from the pool
web_pool stays available, so vs_web keeps sending traffic to 10.1.1.11:80
Node 10.1.1.10 stays up because the pool's HTTP monitor overrides the node monitor
explanation: As the lesson 'Traffic Management Shell (TMSH) and Health Monitors' explains (chapter 'Monitor Status Hierarchy and Examples', 38:59), status flows upward: a down node takes its pool members down, while a pool stays up as long as at least one member is up, and an available pool keeps the virtual server available. So only 10.1.1.10:80 goes down and vs_web continues through 10.1.1.11:80.

stem: A pool uses Priority Group Activation set to 'Less than 2'. Members A and B have priority group 10; members C and D have priority group 5. All four are healthy until member A fails. Where does the BIG-IP send new connections?
options: Only to member B, because group 10 still has an available member
Only to members C and D, because group 10 is now considered failed
To member B and to members C and D, because the available members in the highest group fell below 2
To all members including A, because Priority Group Activation ignores monitor status
explanation: As the lesson 'Traffic Management Shell (TMSH) and Health Monitors' explains (chapter 'Traffic Processing Objects and Load Balancing Methods', 14:05), higher-priority members receive traffic first and lower-priority members are activated when the available higher-priority members drop below the trigger, here less than two. With only B left in group 10, the BIG-IP adds group 5 (C and D) while B keeps receiving traffic, rather than abandoning B.

stem: Which two load-balancing methods are dynamic, adjusting their decisions to current server conditions? (Choose two)
options: Round Robin
Least Connections (member)
Ratio (member)
Observed (member)
Ratio (node)
explanation: As the lesson 'Traffic Management Shell (TMSH) and Health Monitors' explains (chapter 'Traffic Processing Objects and Load Balancing Methods', 14:05), static methods such as Round Robin and Ratio follow predefined settings, while dynamic methods such as Least Connections, Fastest, Observed, Predictive and Dynamic Ratio are decided on the fly. Ratio stays static whether it is applied per member or per node.

stem: A pool uses Ratio (member) with member A set to ratio 3 and member B set to ratio 1. Both are healthy, and the pool receives 8 new connections. How many does member A receive?
explanation: As the lesson 'F5 LTM Traffic Processing, Load Balancing, NAT and SNAT' explains (chapter 'Static Load Balancing Methods: Round Robin and Ratio', 25:38), Ratio distributes connections in proportion to the configured weights, so 3:1 sends three connections to A for every one to B: 6 of 8 to A and 2 to B. An even 4 and 4 split would be Round Robin.

stem: Which two statements about BIG-IP dynamic load-balancing methods are correct? (Choose two)
options: Predictive uses only the current connection count and ignores performance trends
Fastest favours members with the fewest outstanding Layer 7 requests, and without a Layer 7 profile on the virtual server it behaves like Least Connections
Observed requires the administrator to set a static ratio on each member
Round Robin adapts its distribution to server response time
Dynamic Ratio adjusts member weights from performance data collected from the servers, for example through SNMP
explanation: As the lesson 'F5 LTM Traffic Processing, Load Balancing, NAT and SNAT' explains (chapter 'Dynamic Load Balancing Methods: Least Connections, Fastest, Observed, Predictive, Dynamic Ratio', 28:17), Fastest needs a Layer 7 profile to count outstanding requests and otherwise acts like Least Connections, and Dynamic Ratio changes ratios on the fly from server metrics such as SNMP. Predictive differs from Observed precisely because it considers whether a server's performance is improving over time.

stem: Servers S1 and S2 each host HTTP and FTP. S1 currently has 5 HTTP and 50 FTP connections; S2 has 20 HTTP and 0 FTP connections. The HTTP pool uses Least Connections (node). Which server receives the next HTTP connection, and why?
options: S1, because it has fewer HTTP connections (5 versus 20)
S1, because Least Connections (node) ignores FTP traffic
Either server, because node-level methods fall back to Round Robin
S2, because it has fewer connections in total across all services on the node (20 versus 55)
explanation: As the lesson 'F5 LTM Traffic Processing, Load Balancing, NAT and SNAT' explains (chapter 'Load Balancing: Member vs. Node Level Configuration', 33:41), a node-level method counts all connections to the server's IP address across every service, so S1 has 55 and S2 has 20 and S2 wins. With Least Connections (member) only the HTTP service would count, and S1 with 5 connections would be chosen.
